description_ru: Педантичная налоговая консультантка покупает дом с загадочным садом, где на каждом дереве растёт по одному яблоку. Это история о счастливых днях.
text:
When Marguerite Lund bought the house at Number Nine, the estate agent mentioned the roof, the drains, and the unfortunate wallpaper, but not the orchard, perhaps because it seemed too absurd to be a selling point. It occupied the whole of the back garden: thirty-three trees, gnarled and leaning, arranged in rows so crooked they appeared to have been planted by a committee in the middle of an argument.

She was a tax accountant, a woman of orderly habits and modest expectations, and she had no idea what to do with an orchard. She mowed round the trees. She stared at them from the kitchen. In October, to her mild irritation, they began to bear fruit.

It was not ordinary fruit. Each tree produced precisely one apple, and no two apples were alike. One was the colour of a bruise, another a pale, translucent green; one, faintly furry, like a peach with a grudge. Beneath the third tree she found a small enamelled tag, wired to the trunk, and on it a name in copperplate: "Wednesday, 1962."

Marguerite did not believe in the supernatural. She believed in receipts. But she was also, fatally, a methodical woman, and methodical women go looking for records. She found one in the attic, in a tin trunk under a sleeping bag: a leather notebook, thirty-three pages, each headed with a date and each describing, in the same unhurried hand, a single day.

"The morning the Hendersons' boy came home from the sea," read the first. "We ate nothing, and it was the best breakfast of my life." The second described a thunderstorm and a quarrel and, in a postscript, its mending. The third described a dog. It was the sort of ordinary, unremarkable day that evaporates by the following week, except that someone had carefully pressed it into a tree.

She read all night. By dawn she understood, with the dizzy clarity that follows insomnia, that the previous owner, a Mr. Alder, had grafted each of his happiest days onto a tree, and that the trees, being obliging, had fruited accordingly. She went into the garden in her dressing gown and bit into the pale green apple. It tasted of rain on warm stone and of someone laughing in another room.

She sat down on the wet grass and, to her great surprise, cried.

That winter she did something her colleagues considered alarming. She took a Thursday off. It was, objectively, a nothing of a day: a walk, a conversation with a stranger at a bus stop about the price of eggs, a sandwich eaten in the sun. But when she returned, she took the notebook and, under the thirty-third entry, wrote the thirty-fourth, in her small, accountant's script.

In April she bought a sapling, and a spade, and a tag.

The estate agent, who passed the house some years later, said afterwards that the orchard looked remarkably well, although, he added, he could never get the numbers to add up. There seemed to be a new tree every season, and no one at all who admitted to planting them.

focus_sounds.tip_ru: θ: кончик языка слегка между зубами, воздух проходит без голоса: thirty, Thursday, methodical.
r: язык не касается нёба, кончик загнут назад; не раскатывайте русское «р»: trees, orchard.
ŋ: задняя часть языка к нёбу, воздух через нос, без «г»: morning, planting.
Конечное l: кончик языка упирается в дёсны, а звук густой, без русского мягкого «ль»: apple, pale.

questions.question: What was unusual about the trees at Number Nine?
questions.answer: Each bore exactly one different apple.

questions.question: What did she find in the attic?
questions.answer: A leather notebook describing happy days.
